title: When Impostor Syndrome is structural
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Prompted by being repeatedly overlooked for professional opportunities, Hughes argues that impostor syndrome is too often treated as a private psychological quirk when it is at least partly a social experience shaped by class background and institutional context. Drawing on systematic reviews showing wildly inconsistent prevalence estimates (9% to 82%) and sociological research linking impostorism to lower-social-class origins, she shares her own story - first in her family to attend university, learning at 24 that her father was not biologically hers, and being rejected by her biological father - to illustrate how impostor feelings can be rooted in early, structural exclusion rather than individual irrationality. She rejects both wallowing and simple individualised fixes, proposing three institutional responses: making the hidden curriculum explicit, building confidence through schema and rehearsal rather than reassurance, and creating psychologically safe environments where uncertainty is normalised.
points: Hughes's central claim - that impostor syndrome is 'at least partly a social experience' rather than purely an individual psychological trait - reframes a widely individualised concept as structurally produced.

She cites sociological research linking lower-social-class backgrounds to heightened impostor concerns, arguing these feelings can help reproduce inequality by making people doubt whether they truly belong.

Her personal disclosure - being the first in her family at university, learning her father wasn't biological, being rejected by her birth father - grounds the structural argument in lived, specific experience.

Her three proposed institutional responses (explicit hidden curriculum, confidence via schema/rehearsal rather than reassurance, normalised uncertainty) move the argument from diagnosis to concrete leadership action.
quotes: Impostor syndrome is one of those phrases that has become so culturally portable that it now explains everything and, therefore, almost nothing. The problem is not that the term is useless. The problem is that it is often treated as a private psychological quirk when, for many people, it is at least partly a social experience.

A large systematic review found prevalence estimates ranging from 9% to 82%, which tells you two things straight away: first, the experience is common; second, the measurement and definition are highly inconsistent.
Lower-social-class backgrounds are associated with heightened concerns about being an impostor, and that these feelings can help reproduce inequality by making people doubt whether they truly belong.

If you work or study in a culture with low belonging, weak mentoring, high comparison, vague expectations and constant judgement, then you have created ideal conditions for impostor feelings to thrive.

If we want to address impostor syndrome seriously, then the task is not simply to make individuals think more positively. It is to build institutions in which fewer people need to spend quite so much energy convincing themselves they belong.
